title: Must Be True, Must Be False and Inference
summary: No argument to attack, just facts to combine. The right answer is forced by the statements; Must Be False flips it to the one that can't be true.

slides.title: Stay inside the facts
body: These stimuli are statements, not arguments. Treat every one as true and find what they force. Nothing outside the text counts.
Must Be True: the answer is guaranteed by the statements. Must Be False (CANNOT be true): the answer contradicts them. Everything else is a “could be”, and could-be choices are wrong on both.
slides.callout: Prove it with a quote. If you can’t point to the words that force it, it isn’t the answer.

slides.title: How you’ll see it
stems: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?
If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following? (see the Most Strongly Supported deck)

steps.label: Collect the facts
steps.do: Read every statement. Translate conditionals and quantifiers (all, some, most, none) as you go.

steps.label: Combine
steps.do: Look for statements that share a term and chain them. That combination is usually the answer.

steps.label: Light prediction
steps.do: You may not predict the exact answer; know what follows, then go hunting.

steps.label: Prove or kill
steps.do: For each choice: can I point to the words that force it? Strong words (all, never, most) need strong support.

steps.label: For CANNOT
steps.do: Look for the choice that contradicts a fact or the chain. A choice that just isn’t supported can still be true.

slides.title: Level 1: one chain, two links
slides.stimulus: At the Harbor Library, every volunteer is a retired teacher. Every retired teacher who volunteers there has completed a background check before starting. The library holds a book sale each spring. Priya volunteers at the Harbor Library, and she began last month.
slides.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Priya taught school for more than ten years before she retired from the classroom.
choices.B: Every retired teacher in town has completed a background check before applying to volunteer.
choices.C: Priya completed a background check before she began volunteering at the library.
choices.D: Anyone who has completed a background check at the library is a volunteer at the library.
choices.E: Most of the library's volunteers help to run the library's spring book sale.

steps.label: Collect the facts
steps.note: Volunteers are retired teachers. Retired teachers who volunteer have had a background check. Priya volunteers.
steps.highlight: Priya volunteers at the Harbor Library, and she began last month.

steps.label: Combine
steps.note: Priya volunteers, so she is a retired teacher. That makes her a retired teacher who volunteers there, and every such person has had the check.
steps.highlight: every volunteer is a retired teacher

steps.label: Prove or kill
steps.note: Only C can be pointed to in the text. The others add years, towns, reversed arrows or a book sale the facts never link to volunteers.

why.A: Unsupported. Nothing says how long Priya taught.
why.B: Too strong. The check is stated only for retired teachers who volunteer at the library, not for every retired teacher in town.
why.C: Correct. Priya is a volunteer, so she is a retired teacher who volunteers there, and every such person completed the check before starting.
why.D: Reversed conditional. Volunteers have had the check; the text does not say everyone with a check volunteers.
why.E: Unsupported. The book sale is mentioned once and never tied to the volunteers.

slides.title: Level 2: the method, step by step
slides.stimulus: Every chef at Marlow's restaurant trained at the Lyon Institute. Some of the chefs at Marlow's also teach evening cooking classes. No one who teaches evening cooking classes works the late shift at Marlow's.
slides.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: No one who trained at the Lyon Institute works the late shift at Marlow's.
choices.B: Every chef at Marlow's who teaches evening classes trained somewhere other than the Lyon Institute.
choices.C: Most chefs at Marlow's work the late shift.
choices.D: Some chefs at Marlow's who work the late shift teach evening classes.
choices.E: Some people who trained at the Lyon Institute do not work the late shift at Marlow's.

steps.label: Translate
steps.note: Marlow's chef → Lyon. Some Marlow's chefs teach evening classes. Evening teacher → not late shift.

steps.label: Combine
steps.note: The chefs who teach evening classes trained at Lyon and don't work the late shift.
steps.highlight: Some of the chefs at Marlow's also teach evening cooking classes.

steps.label: So
steps.note: At least some Lyon-trained people don't work the late shift. Hunt for that.

steps.label: Spot the CANNOTs
steps.note: B and D contradict the facts. On a Must Be False version of this question, either would be the answer.

why.A: Too strong. Lyon-trained chefs who don't teach could work the late shift.
why.B: Contradicts the first statement: every Marlow's chef trained at Lyon. This one cannot be true.
why.D: Contradicts the third statement: evening teachers don't work the late shift. Cannot be true.
why.E: Correct. The chefs who teach evening classes are Lyon-trained and off the late shift.

slides.title: Level 3: a quantifier carried down a chain
slides.stimulus: A survey of the Orsen Valley growers' co-op produced the following findings for the most recent season. Growers may sell at one market, at both, or at neither. Every grower who sells at the Saturday market is certified organic. Most Saturday-market growers also sell at the Wednesday market. Every grower who sells at the Wednesday market irrigates exclusively by drip. No grower who irrigates exclusively by drip buys water rights from the district. Several growers who are not certified organic do buy water rights.
slides.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Some growers who sell at the Saturday market do not buy water rights from the district.
choices.B: Every grower who irrigates exclusively by drip also sells at the Wednesday market of the co-op.
choices.C: No certified-organic grower in the whole valley buys water rights from the district.
choices.D: Most growers who buy water rights from the district also sell at the Saturday market.
choices.E: Every grower who sells at the Wednesday market also sells at the Saturday market of the co-op.

steps.label: Translate
steps.note: Saturday (S) means organic. Most S also sell Wednesday (W). W means drip only. Drip only means no water rights.
steps.highlight: Most Saturday-market growers also sell at the Wednesday market.

steps.label: Chain the arrows
steps.note: Follow W forward: W then drip only, then no water rights. Every Wednesday seller buys no water rights.

steps.label: Carry 'most' through the chain
steps.note: Most S are W, and every W buys no rights. So most S buy no rights. Most guarantees at least some, which is the key's wording.

steps.label: Name the traps
steps.note: B and E read an arrow backwards. C stretches the last sentence: the word 'No' kills it, because the text says only that some non-organic growers buy rights.
steps.highlight: Several growers who are not certified organic do buy water rights.

steps.label: Confirm
steps.note: D flips 'most of S' into 'most of the buyers'. Only A has a quote behind it.

why.A: Correct. Most Saturday growers sell on Wednesday, and no Wednesday seller buys water rights, so more than half of them, and therefore at least some, buy none.
why.B: Reversed conditional. Every Wednesday seller irrigates by drip, but drip growers need not sell on Wednesday.
why.C: Too strong. The last sentence names some non-organic buyers; it never says organic growers cannot buy, and organic growers outside the Saturday market are unconstrained.
why.D: Flips the quantifier. Most Saturday growers are non-buyers; nothing says what share of buyers sell on Saturday.
why.E: Reversed. Most Saturday growers also sell on Wednesday, which does not mean every Wednesday seller sells on Saturday.

slides.title: Level 4: a count that blocks a conditional chain
slides.stimulus: The Delmar Foundation, which makes small grants to community groups, has twelve reviewers, and each reviewer rates each proposal independently. Proposals are open to any community group in the region. The foundation funds a proposal only if at least two of its reviewers rate that proposal strong. A reviewer rates a proposal that involves human subjects strong only if that reviewer has completed the foundation's ethics course. Anyone who has completed the ethics course has also served on the foundation's oversight board. This year, exactly one of the twelve reviewers has served on the oversight board.
slides.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.A: A proposal that involves human subjects was rated strong by exactly one reviewer this year.
choices.B: A proposal that involves no human subjects was funded this year.
choices.C: A reviewer who has served on the oversight board has not completed the ethics course.
choices.D: Two proposals that involve human subjects were each rated strong by the same reviewer this year.
choices.E: A proposal that involves human subjects was funded this year.

steps.label: Collect the facts
steps.note: Four rules: funded needs two strong ratings; a strong rating on a human-subjects proposal needs the ethics course; the course means board service; one reviewer has served on the board.
steps.highlight: exactly one of the twelve reviewers has served on the oversight board

steps.label: Chain the conditionals
steps.note: Strong on a human-subjects proposal, then ethics course, then board service. Every such rater must be a board member.

steps.label: Apply the count
steps.note: Only one reviewer is on the board. So at most one reviewer can rate a human-subjects proposal strong, and funding needs two.

steps.label: Spot the CANNOT
steps.note: A human-subjects proposal cannot be funded. Everything else only fails to be forced, so it could be true.

steps.label: Name the trap
steps.note: B looks like E but says 'no human subjects', and the ethics rule never touches those. C reads the arrow backwards: course means board, not board means course.
steps.highlight: A reviewer rates a proposal that involves human subjects strong only if that reviewer has completed the foundation's ethics course.

why.A: Could be true. The one board member can rate it strong; only 'at least two' ratings is blocked.
why.B: Could be true. The ethics rule covers only human-subjects proposals, so any two reviewers may rate this one strong.
why.C: Could be true. The course leads to board service, not the reverse, so the one board member may have skipped the course.
why.D: Could be true. The single reviewer who completed the course can rate several such proposals strong.
why.E: Correct. Funding needs two strong ratings, each rater of a human-subjects proposal must be a board member, and only one reviewer is.

traps.name: Could be true
traps.tell: Fits with the facts but isn’t forced. Wrong on Must Be True and on Must Be False.

traps.name: One word too strong
traps.tell: All where the text gives some; most where it gives many.

traps.name: Real-world reasonable
traps.tell: Sounds sensible but relies on outside knowledge.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Facts, not an argument. Accept all of them.
Chain statements that share a term.
Must Be True: point to the words that force it.
CANNOT be true: find the contradiction, not the unsupported claim.
Could be true is wrong on both.
